articles.text: On Saturday, March 21, Firefighter-Paramedic Robb Hendry retired after 23 years of service with the Piedmont Fire Department. The Fire Department held a ceremony to honor his service at 8 a.m. Saturday morning, at the conclusion of his final shift. In addition to Fire Department staff, the ceremony was attended by Mayor Betsy Andersen, City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, Hendry’s partner Cindy, his son Jack, and retired Piedmont Fire Department Engineer John Tessandori. The ceremony included remarks from Chief Brannigan, Mayor Andersen, and Captain Jon Fitzpatrick. Following the remarks, Chief Brannigan presented Hendry with a flag that flew over the Fire Station during his final shift, and invited Hendry to say a few words. Following the ceremony, the group gathered in the City Hall courtyard for coffee and refreshments. “As your Chief for the past five years, I have come to rely on you as the voice of experience, knowledge, and patience,” said Chief Brannigan. “It takes patience with patients and passion for the craft to spend more than two decades showing up for people having the worst day of their lives. Fighting fire takes grit, strength, courage, and resilience – all characteristics you display day in and day out. You’ve set an example for your colleagues, trainees, and the people of Piedmont. This community is safer for your service, and Robb Hendry was presented with an American flag by Chief Dave Brannigan.

articles.text: At its March Meeting, Trustees and Advisors of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation were presented with two new projects. Option A results from a new law in California prohibiting cities after the end of this year from using drinking water to irrigate “nonfunctional” lawns—that is, grass that has no recreational or community purpose. Option B expands upon PBF’s project from last fall to install new swings in the tot lot near the Exedra. It will create a mulched area adjacent to the new swings for nature and adventure play. The City staff has determined that many areas of lawn will be affected by the prohibition on using drinking water for grass. The project contemplates replacing the lawns with water-wise, attractive native plants, resulting in a dramatic reduction in water use while educating Piedmont residents on how their lawns can likewise be transformed into environmentally friendly, attractive gardens. Choice B is already under construction. Two dying Redwood trees in Piedmont Park had to be removed, and sections have already been sawn into stepping stones to be installed near the tot lot. Additionally, PBF has already determined to plant two new Dogwood trees in that area in memory of Sue Herrick, longtime member of the PBF Board and past President of PBF, as well as Chair of the Park Commission. PBF voted to contribute $15,000 from its general funds to support the lawn conversion project and use the Spring Campaign to support the mulched nature play area next to the tot lot and new swings. The nature area will greatly enhance the play opportunities, complementing the swing project, which was extremely popular with donors. The City reported that construction of the Dearing Memorial will begin soon. PBF’s campaign in support of this project is nearing its goal, and the Spring Brochure will note that contributions can put it over the top. Last, but certainly not least, the City reminded all that the opening of the new swimming pool complex will occur on April 11. PBF was the second-largest contributor to this project after Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO). Its contribution funded the spectacular plantings that dramatically enhance the complex. Not only is the planting attractive, but most importantly, it requires low water use and is easy to maintain. Residents can expect to receive PBF’s Spring Brochure later this spring. In the meantime, donations to any of the above-referenced projects can be made immediately by mail to PBF at the Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont, 94611, or by visiting its website at www. articles.text: Editor: I’m glad to read that Piedmont’s Chief Shavies is collaborating with other law enforcement agencies throughout our region to stop catalytic converter thefts. The thugs on the street who steal the “cats” sell them to chop shops. The chop shops take out the valuable metals and sell them to refineries or fences. Stop the flow of money from the top of the pyramid and the crime on the street will subside. It’s a regional, or even a statewide problem requiring cooperation of law enforcement at every level of government. May it continue, with even more vigor. –Bruce Joffe

articles.text: Opening month hours, $5 drop-ins, and annual pass sales As the April 11 opening of Piedmont’s new Community Pool nears, here’s what to expect during the first month of operations. On opening day, Friday, April 11, the pool will be open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with open swim available all day. From April 11 through April 30, everyone can swim for $5 per visit. Throughout April, both the competition and activity pools will offer lap swim and open swim daily. The competition pool will be set up primarily for lap swim during morning hours, with a limited number of lanes available later in the day. In the activity pool, lap swim will be available 6 - 9:30 a.m. on weekdays and 7 - 10 a.m. on weekends. A full April schedule, including the number of lap lanes available at different times in each pool and when diving boards will be open, will be published at piedmont.ca.gov/pool. Resident annual pass sales began March 24, at 6 p.m., through the City’s Aquatics registration portal at rec.us/piedmont. There is no limit on annual pass sales. If you’re considering an annual pass for your household, take your time to review the options, and reach out if you need help before making a purchase. When pass sales open, you will see options available for the four base pass types – Adult, Senior, Youth, Family – as well as “Adult Couple” and “Senior Couple” options, which are prebuilt versions of the pool’s flexible “Build-a-Pass” structure. If you want a different household mix, start by adding the base pass that best fits your household to your cart. When you proceed to checkout, a pop-up window will give you the option to add household members or other addons. Community members purchasing a pass will also be asked to review and agree to pool rules as part of the checkout process. Aquatics staff are available to answer questions and provide hands-on support with the account setup, pass options, and programming options at upcoming open lobby hours: • Wednesday, March 25: 5 - 6:30 p.m. • Thursday, March 26: 4:30 - 6:30 p.m. • Monday, March 31: 4 - 6 p.m. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont recreation department is hopping into Spring with 2026’s Bunny Blast. The egg hunt will feature over 5000 stuffed eggs for children to search for. The colorful eggs filled with sweet surprises and seasonal activities will be hosted in the park. The Egg hunts will take place at different times for each age group. Below is the hunt’s schedule: • 2 Years: 9:45 a.m. • 3 Years: 10:00 a.m. • 4 & 5 Years: 10:15 a.m. • 6 & 7 Years: 10:30 a.m. Advanced registration is required. Honolulu and Dallas are sweet, sensitive sisters who are deeply devoted to each other — snuggling, grooming, and staying close throughout the day — and seeking a patient guardian to help them blossom. These girls start off quite shy, so will appreciate a calm home and an experienced adopter who can go at their pace. Dallas, in particular, takes her time to observe before she decides she feel safe, eventually indulging in cozy lounging, gentle pets, and quiet companionship near you. Her meow is a little smaller than Honolulu’s, but it is mighty. Honolulu is a fun gal who uses a daily inhaler to keep her asthma well-managed — but that doesn’t slow her down. This playful, chatty, gal will follow you from room to room, carrying her blue sparkle ball in her mouth, and asking for Adopt Honolulu and Dallas through Cat Town. pets or play (sometimes both at once). She’s affectionate, curious, and loves to be involved in whatever you’re doing. Honolulu and Dallas are 5 years old, spayed, vaccinated, and microchipped. articles.text: The 2026 White Elephant Sale are revealed: $3,328,687 raised The 67th annual White Elephant Sale (WES), held from late January to early March 2026, raised a record-breaking $3.3 million to benefit the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA). This marks the highest earnings in the sale’s history, surpassing last year’s record-breaking proceeds of $2.9 million. A portion of the proceeds provide critical support to OMCA’s exhibitions, programs, and operations. Organized and presented by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, the White Elephant Sale is the largest annual fundraising event for OMCA. “What a truly great year for the White Elephant Sale,” said Judy Wilkinson, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. “Reaching a new fundraising milestone in our 67th year speaks to the passion, generosity, and sheer joy that the community brings to this event. It’s inspiring to see our donors, volunteers, employees, and shoppers rally around the Museum in such a powerful way.” “This remarkable achievement reflects the strength of a partnership that has shaped OMCA for nearly seven decades,” said Lori Fogarty, Executive Director and CEO of OMCA. “Because of the tireless work of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and their dedicated volunteers, we are able to deepen the Museum’s impact—expanding access, amplifying California stories, and creating welcoming spaces for our community to gather. We are deeply grateful.” In recent years, the White Elephant Sale has consistently raised over $2 million annually. The sale continues to offer a lively in-person shopping experience, attracting thousands of shoppers each year and providing an opportunity for the community to come together in support of the Museum. The White Elephant Sale’s success depends on generous public donations, with a wide range of gently used, high-quality items accepted year-round. For updates on how to donate, including a list of items that cannot be accepted, please visit the White Elephant Sale website. Plans for the 68th annual White Elephant Sale in 2027 are already underway, setting the stage for another impactful year of fundraising in support of OMCA’s mission to tell the diverse stories of California and to build more equitable and connected communities. About the Oakland Museum Women’s Board The sole mission of The Oakland Museum Women’s Board (OMWB) is to raise money to support the Oakland Museum of California’s acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since 1959, the OMWB has contributed nearly $34 million to the Museum. Nearly 1,000 dedicated volunteers work year-round to organize and present the White Elephant Sale, which attracts shoppers from the Bay Area and beyond. About the Oakland Museum of California Founded in 1969 as the “museum of the people,” the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) tells the diverse stories of California’s art, history, and natural environment. Through inclusive exhibitions, public programs, and educational initiatives, OMCA creates space for meaningful dialogue and strives to build more equitable, empathetic, and connected communities. With more than 2 million objects, OMCA’s collection of art, history, and natural science is a resource for understanding California’s dynamic heritage— all within its 110,000-squarefeet of gallery space and seven-acre campus. A leading Bay Area cultural institution rooted in Oakland, OMCA is dedicated to fostering an environment where visitors from the region, state, and beyond feel valued and empowered to shape the future of California’s cultural landscape. Oakland Museum Women’s Board President, Judy Wilkinson, and White Elephant Sale Chair, Mary Retzinger enjoy the celebration of a successful year.

articles.text: Vanessa Lujan AI is here, but its arrival in schools has been anything but straightforward. A teacher reads an essay and wonders how much of it is her student’s thinking. A district leader sits through another pitch for an “AI-powered solution” without a clear way to evaluate it. A student uses a tool that can explain almost anything—except how it works. Across classrooms and communities, AI is not just a new resource; it is a source of unease. AI literacy is becoming a core K-12 responsibility It goes far beyond using the latest tools. It means asking questions that enable informed choices: how AI systems work, what data they rely on, and how to evaluate their outputs. It also includes critical attention to risks and limitations, how bias can enter, what privacy protections matter, and how to keep human judgment at the center. The challenge for schools and districts is that AI is not arriving as a single initiative to adopt or Learning at The Lawrence Hall of Science reject. It is arriving across tools, classrooms, and workflows—and constantly changing. Without a coherent approach and shared vision there is fragmentation, and districts struggle to develop strategy or communicate clearly with educators, families, boards, and community partners. AI is seen as a source of unease By Eric Greenwald and Vanessa Lujan AI is here, but its arrival in schools has been anything but straightforward. A teacher reads an essay and wonders how much of it is her student’s thinking. A district leader sits through another pitch for an “AI-powered solution” without a clear way to evaluate it. A student uses a tool that can explain almost anything—except how it works. Across classrooms and communities, AI is not just a new resource; it is a source of unease. AI literacy is becoming a core K-12 responsibility It goes far beyond using the latest tools. It means asking questions that enable informed choices: how AI systems work, what data they rely on, and how to evaluate their outputs. It also includes critical attention to risks and limitations, how bias can enter, what privacy protections matter, and how to keep human judgment at the center. The challenge for schools and districts is that AI is not arriving as a single initiative to adopt or Learning at The Lawrence Hall of Science reject. It is arriving across tools, classrooms, and workflows—and constantly changing. Without a coherent approach and shared vision there is fragmentation, and districts struggle to develop strategy or communicate clearly with educators, families, boards, and community partners. We have been out listening We have been holding conversations with district leaders, educators, and thought leaders to understand what matters most. At a recent gathering of the California African American Superintendents Association, for example, we met with leaders who carry the daily responsibility of protecting students, building trust, and delivering results. articles.text: Dress Best for Less (DBFL) has announced a generous donation of $30,000 to the PUSD Wellness Center. The gift will strengthen mental health support for Piedmont students by fully offsetting the cost of a Wellness Center counselor for the 2026-27 academic year. The PUSD Wellness Center serves students at Piedmont High School, Piedmont Middle School, and Millennium High School, providing a safe space where expert staff can connect students to the right level of counseling and wellness support at no cost to families. During the previous school year, the Wellness Center provided over 2,000 hours of therapy for students, and delivered hundreds of hours of additional support during student drop-ins. The DBFL donation will help ensure that PUSD students continue to benefit from mental health and wellness support, whether they need a brief check-in, short-term counseling during a stressful period or longer-term care. Wellness Center leaders announced the DBFL donation during a parent panel discussion on student wellness and academic stress hosted by the PUSD Wellness Center on Monday, January 26. The evening’s program, which featured mental health experts from a range of disciplines, explored how mental health and wellness challenges PUSD Wellness Center’s January 26 event on student wellbeing featured panelists Martin Diller (left), LMFT; Lauren Hartman, M.D.; Brian Clark, Psy.D.; Naomi Edelson, Psy.D.; and Sari Sanghvi, Ph.D. can show up in students’ lives and what families, educators and peers can do to support them. During the program, DBFL President Nagisa Yamamoto spoke about the DBFL’s commitment to supporting Piedmont youth. “DBFL is thrilled to support the needs of the Piedmont students through this donation,” Yamamoto said. “We feel it will help the well-being of many, many students.” In addition to providing mental health and wellness support for PUSD students, the Wellness Center is also an important training site for future mental health professionals as a member of the Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium. Each year, the PUSD Wellness Center welcomes a small group of graduate student counseling interns from UC Berkeley, The Wright Institute, the University of San Francisco, and Saint Mary’s College of Moraga. The counseling interns are selected from a national pool of applicants and represent diverse social, ethnic, and gender expansive groups. These internship positions expand the Wellness Center’s student support capacity while preparing clinicians for career pathways in youth mental health. The Wellness Center’s mission is grounded in the philosophy that caring for student mental health and wellness strengthens the entire school community. When students have the support they need, they can bring more focus to the classroom, build healthier relationships and carry coping skills far beyond graduation. With DBFL’s generous gift, Piedmont’s support system for student wellness is stronger than ever for the year ahead. For more information about the PUSD Wellness Center, or to donate, please visit Piedmontwellness.org.

articles.text: With new Scouts joining troops this time of year, we asked a few senior Scouts to look back on their journeys. Here’s what they loved most, and the memories that stand out. Theo Ferguson Eagle Scout, Troop 11 What I love the most about Scouting is that I’ve met some amazing and inspiring people that I never would have known otherwise. articles.text: Staff Photos Hallie Burden sends in a shot against Justin-Siena. She helped changed the game as the faceoff specialist. It was a big week for Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team, winning its first two matches of the season. They recently beat Justin-Siena 13-8 on Friday, March 20 at Witter Field and won 8-7 over Dougherty Valley on Tuesday, March 17, also at home. Piedmont trailed Justin-Siena 5-1 early in the second quarter, but went on a 10-goal scoring run to take a commanding 11-5 lead. “Hallie [Burden] adjusted how she was taking the draw and it made a big impact. We chased down every ground ball, but the draw control was a huge difference. We had three really good practices and it’s just been about getting the girls on the same page,” explained coach Carlton Chan. “We realized we needed to take time on transitions and once we get on attack we could get our goals,” senior captain Peyton Watson added. Winning in the faceoff circle proved to be a catalyst in their victory. After losing the first six draws of the game, Hallie Burden helped win 10 of the next 11 attempts. “I figured out if their draw taker was going softer or harder. I noticed she was going hard so I stayed patient, pull back, and then go for it,” Burden said. Piedmont did well adjusting in the match, playing physically on the attack and creating space to shoot with swift moves and cuts around defenders. “We were in a slump and we’ve just been able to relax more. We’re figuring out how to have fun with it, creating more space, and just helping each other,” Watson said. 13-8 over Justin-Siena Justin-Siena scored the game’s first two goals before Watson scored from a shooting space opportunity with 4:35 left in the quarter. From there, the Braves scored three straight to take a 5-1 lead 30 seconds into the second quarter at 11:30. But Piedmont’s comeback was on from there. Watson sent in a shot at the 4:37 mark, and then Watson scored 32 seconds later. Burden scored with 3:48 left, and then Peyton Watson scored five goals against Justin-Siena. Sydney Latvala (right) had a 3-goal hat trick against Justin-Siena. In the photo she is shown celebrating a goal with Zoya Schulze. Watson assisted Burden with 2:05 left to not the game up at 5-5. Zoya Schulze then assisted Watson to send in a shot from close distance as time expired, giving PHS a 6-5 lead at halftime. Piedmont’s onslaught continued in the third. Burden scored one minute in, then Watson scored 40 seconds later. Sydney Latvala scored from a shooting space chance with 9:14 left, while Schulze did the same two minutes later. Burden scored with five minutes left to give PHS a commanding 11-5 lead. JSHS finally scored again with 3:50 left in the third, while Latvala scored again with 1:04 remaining. In the fourth, Burden assisted Latvala for her hat trick with 7:05 left for Piedmont’s final goal. Justin-Siena scored the game’s final two goals at 1:57 and 1:06. Final stats: Watson had five goals, one assist, and scooped one ground ball. Burden scored four goals, one assist, and won three draws. Latvala scored three and won five draws. Schulze had a goal, assist, and won three draws. 8-7 over Dougherty Valley Both teams finished the first quarter tied 2-2, while PHS took a 5-3 lead by halftime. DVHS got one back in the third, trailing 5-4, while both teams added three goals in the final going. Piedmont had four different players score two goals. Final stats: Schulze had two goals, won two draws, and a ground ball. Watson had two goals and one ground ball. Latvala scored twice and had one ground ball. Burden scored two, won two draws, and three ground balls. Tuesday vs. Lick-Wilmerding Piedmont hosted Lick-Wilmerding on Tuesday, March 24. details. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two different events on Friday, and Saturday, March 20-21: the Dublin Distance Fiesta at Dublin HS and the Swenson/Werne Invitational at San Ramon Valley HS in Danville. The Dublin Distance Fiesta is one of the marquee events of the spring season for distance runners; it has now been running for 19 years and brings together hundreds of schools and thousands of distance runners. The Swensen/ Werne Invitational, meanwhile, is the previous SRV Sprint & Field Festival, marking the second year of its re-brand. Sebastien Swain continued his strong return from a knee injury, finishing 23rd in a field of 1,341 runners in the 1600 meters, clocking a time of 4:21.85. “Seb’s right where we expect him to be. He was happy with the 4:21 mile and so were we. The key is that he hit 3:13 after 1200 meters so he set himself up for a 4:15 mile. He’s only been fully working out for a few weeks, so he’s on his way,” Assadi said. On the girls’ side, senior leader Skylar Best had a strong 68th place finish in the 800 of 734 athletes, coming across the line in 2:26.42. Leighton Mand, meanwhile, was 92nd of 711 in the 1600 in 5:19.94. “Skylar and Leighton have been a nice tag team this season. Their races were encouraging on Saturday and it feels like they’re fully in mid-season form,” Assadi said. Swensen/Werne Invitational At the Swensen/Werne Invitational, it was a strong showing by Rehan Mumtaz in two events with personal best times. He was fifth of 155 sprinters in the 100 meters in 11.12 seconds, and was eighth of 98 in the 200 in 22.67. Claire Aubrecht also continued to prove her status as a top sprinter. She was seventh of 126 runners in the 100 with a personal best time of 12.67, and was ninth of 83 in the 200 in 26.31. “Rehan’s taking the classic junior year leap but taking it to another level. He’s red hot. Claire hit another PR in the 100, she’s going to keep doing some damage in the events coming up,” Assadi said. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team is seeking its first win in four games. It’s been a rough stretch in March for Piedmont’s baseball team, which is seeking its first win since March 4 against HeadRoyce. Over the past week, Piedmont tied Moreau Catholic 4-4 at Raimondi Park in Oakland on Saturday, March 21, lost 11-7 to Albany at Humphries Diamond on Friday, March 20, and lost 12-8 at Miramonte in Orinda on Tuesday, March 17. “We’re playing really good teams that are putting the bat on the ball,” said coach Eric Olson. “Miramonte hit four home runs on us, Albany got a bunch of extra base hits today. I believe in our pitchers, we’re just a little off right now. We’re leaving balls up and they’re taking advantage of it.” The batch of results brings Piedmont’s record to 2-3-2 (W-L-T). The team has time to get things back on track with 17 games left in its regular season. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of their league schedule in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. They played their first of a twogame series against Castro Valley yesterday, March 24, and face the Trojans again on Thursday, March 26. 4-4 with Moreau Piedmont scored twice in the top of the first inning, while Moreau got to the front with individual runs in the bottom of the first, second, and third. PHS took Staff Photos a 4-3 lead in the top of the sixth, but Moreau tied things up in the bottom of the seventh. In the top of the first, Diego Delventhal got Piedmont on the board with a two-run homer. Final stats: Diego Delventhal went 3-for-4 with a run scored, four RBIs, a double and a home run. Lucas Delventhal went 2-for-4 with a run scored. Diego Delventhal had a home run against Moreau, a triple against Albany, and a double against Miramonte.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 25, 2026 13 Track & Field team competes at Dublin Distance, Swenson/Werne Invitational By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two different events on Friday, and Saturday, March 20-21: the Dublin Distance Fiesta at Dublin HS and the Swenson/Werne Invitational at San Ramon Valley HS in Danville. The Dublin Distance Fiesta is one of the marquee events of the spring season for distance runners; it has now been running for 19 years and brings together hundreds of schools and thousands of distance runners. The Swensen/ Werne Invitational, meanwhile, is the previous SRV Sprint & Field Festival, marking the second year of its re-brand. Sebastien Swain continued his strong return from a knee injury, finishing 23rd in a field of 1,341 runners in the 1600 meters, clocking a time of 4:21.85. “Seb’s right where we expect him to be. He was happy with the 4:21 mile and so were we. The key is that he hit 3:13 after 1200 meters so he set himself up for a 4:15 mile. He’s only been fully working out for a few weeks, so he’s on his way,” Assadi said. On the girls’ side, senior leader Skylar Best had a strong 68th place finish in the 800 of 734 athletes, coming across the line in 2:26.42. Leighton Mand, meanwhile, was 92nd of 711 in the 1600 in 5:19.94. “Skylar and Leighton have been a nice tag team this season. Their races were encouraging on Saturday and it feels like they’re fully in mid-season form,” Assadi said. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team put together an impressive showing in their meet against Bishop O’Dowd, highlighted by a strong performance from the varsity boys and a number of standout individual swims. The Piedmont varsity boys secured a decisive 110–49 victory over Bishop O’Dowd, while the varsity girls lost 115-45. Coach Elizabeth Dally emphasized pride in the team’s overall effort and competitiveness throughout the meet. Dally highlighted several swimmers who led the way in scoring. “Our top point scorers for varsity were Cole Carnazzo and Sam White with 12 points each, and Dima Secor, Connor Carnazzo, and Asher Takazawa with 10 points each. He clocked a time of 1:00.39 in the 100 breaststroke a field of five, and put up a 53.65 in the 100 fly against three other swimmers. His younger brother, Connor Carnazzo, won the 200 freestyle with a time of 1:55.15 against three other swimmers. Dima Secor won the 200 individual medley with a time of 1:57.26 in a field of four. He was also second of five in the 100 breast in 1:05.28. Asher Takazawa won the 100 backstroke in 55.89 in a field of five, while Connor Carnazzo was second in 51.01. Sam White of the girls’ team won two individual events. She won the 500 free with a time of 5:41.31 in a field of six. She won the 100 fly in 1:07.92 against two others. articles.text: Youth sports programs don’t always have to be about competition! ANTS Sports has spent years building youth sports programs that combine fun, skill development, and meaningful connection to build a love of sports for a lifetime in an inclusive and non-competitive environment. ANTS has been partnering with the City of Piedmont since 2020, offering unique summer camps and after school enrichment classes. This summer, they’re returning with their popular tennis camps (ages 5-11), volleyball camps, (ages 8-14), and even pickleball camps! Each program is designed to create a fun, safe, and age-appropriate environment where kids feel comfortable trying new things. Whether a child is picking up a racket for the first time or developing more advanced skills, the goal of ANTS programs is to always ensure kids feel supported, encouraged, and excited to participate. Sportsmanship is a fundamental part of sports, and ANTS teaches it through their very own STAR framework: Super Fun, Teamwork, Always Try, and Respect. Whether working together as a team in group activities, supporting one another in pairs, or putting in their best effort in individual skill work, participants use STAR to build character and shape healthy habits that extend far beyond the court. The impact of youth sports programs goes well beyond skill development. Participating in team-based activities fosters social-emotional learning, teaching kids how to communicate, collaborate, and navigate individual and interpersonal challenges. ANTS coaches, with their years of experience and genuine love for sports, serve as positive role models and mentors, helping to inspire and guide children in both athletic and personal growth throughout each and every program. In a time when screen time often competes with active play, youth sports programs offer kids the chance to get outside and move, connect, and build confidence in a positive community. ANTS Sports is proud to share this opportunity with kids in Piedmont all year round! Register for PRD ANTS programs on Community Pass and find more information about ANTS Sports at www.antssports.com. Hands in! ANTS camps always end with a team cheer. Building a team and making new friends is the best part of sports.

articles.text: “New Japanese Clay” is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through June. The exhibition brings together modern and contemporary works that reimagine a centuries-old tradition in Japanese ceramics. Infused with vivid color and sculptural ambition, the pieces range from rugged, earthbound forms that evoke stone and soil to delicate constructions that appear as light as paper or billowing fabric. Museum officials said the exhibition reflects both Japan’s rich ceramic history and the increasingly global nature of contemporary art training and practice, as well as materials used. The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters who are expanding the expressive possibilities of clay. Robert Mintz, who organized the exhibition, said the featured artists build on the legacy of the mingei, or folk art, movement while forging distinctly experimental paths. “The artists in New Japanese Clay are challenging the conventions of functional ceramics and pivoting toward a purely sculptural experience,” Mintz said in a statement. “Their creations are meant to intrigue and delight; the vessel form is just a point of departure for spectacular experimentation.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/new-japanese-clay/. “New Japanese Clay” is on view now through June. Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Cal Performances will welcome The Joffrey Ballet back to Zellerbach Hall in April for three performances of Midsummer Night’s Dream, marking the West Coast premiere of the work by Swedish choreographer Alexander Ekman. The Joffrey Ballet is based in Chicago and is known for blending classical ballet with contemporary work. The company has been the resident dance company at Lyric Opera House since the 2021–22 season and continues an eight-year residency partnership with Cal Performances that began in 2024. Ekman’s Midsummer Night’s Dream takes inspiration from Scandinavian midsummer traditions rather than William Shakespeare’s play of the same name. The production features nearly three dozen dancers, surreal stage design, and a live original score by Swedish composer Mikael Karlsson. Vocals will be performed by Anna von Hausswolff, whose music combines post-rock, minimalism, and pop influences. Additional musicians include percussionist Niklas Brommare and pianist Jorge Ivars, joined by a string quartet. The performances are scheduled for Friday, April 17, at 7 p.m.; Saturday, April 18, at 8 p.m.; and Sunday, April 19, at 3 p.m. The Friday performance will also serve as the centerpiece of Cal Performances at UC Berkeley’s 2026 gala. Tickets are available online at www.calperformances.org or by calling the box office at (510) 642-9988. Photo courtesy of The Joffrey Ballet The Chicago-based ballet company returns to UC Berkeley next month.

articles.text: Youth Ikebana workshop held Sunday Ruth Bancroft gardens, located in Walnut Creek, will host an Ikebana workshop for adults this Saturday, March 28, and a youth workshop on Sunday, March 29. Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arrangements, a tradition that dates back to the Heian period centuries ago. Hands-on workshops follow a demonstration by Pia Horei Groth who will share versatile techniques for creating elegant, architectural arrangements, and specifically how to create a ‘Moribana’ or upright style arrangement. Each student will be provided with plant materials, a suiban (low-vase), and a kenzan (pin-frog) to work with. Clippers will be available and attendees may bring their own tools for arranging. The Saturday workshop is held from 1 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. The garden will also offer an introductory workshop to Ikebana for youth on Sunday, March 29, from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. An additional drop-in demonstration with Sharon Suimei Doi from the Sogetsu San Francisco Bay Area Branch will be held Sunday at 1 p.m. The workshop is presented in conjunction with the ArtScapes in the Garden exhibition, created by Sogetsu San Francisco. The garden and Great Room will feature floral installations made with materials from the garden Thursday, March 26, through Sunday, March 29 during open hours. ‘ArtScapes in the Garden’ is free to explore for Ruth Bancroft members; non-members receive access to the exhibit with regular admission. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/introduction-to-ikebana-workshop/ to register. Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery The workshop is presented in conjunction with the ArtScapes in the Garden exhibition.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft gardens host Japanese floral art workshop this Saturday

articles.text: Jazz pianist Monty Alexander Monty Alexander, a Jamaican-born jazz pianist and bebop virtuoso, performs at Miner Auditorium in San Francisco this Sunday, March 29. Born and raised in Kingston, Jamaica, Alexander took his first piano lessons at age six and was often invited to sit in with the bands of prominent musicians working in Jamaican nightclubs and hotels. His career, which spans more than three decades, includes work with Frank Sinatra, Ray Brown, Dizzy Gillespie, Sonny Rollins, Quincy Jones, Ernest Ranglin, Sly Dunbar, and Robbie Shakespeare. He eventually formed a band called “Monty and the Cyclones,” which landed several songs on the Jamaican music charts between 1958 to 1960. Alexander has recorded over 40 albums since then, each influenced by his Caribbean roots. In 2022, Alexander received the Order of Jamaica by the Jamaican government for “Sterling Contributions to the Promotions of Jamaican Music and the Jazz Genre Interpretations Globally”. His latest release, 2024’s D-Day, is a collection of compositions based on the historic day that saw the pivotal Allied invasion of France in WWII, also Alexander’s birthday. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/25-26/monty-alexander/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: World-renowned pianist Yuja Wang performs with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra at Davies Symphony Hall on April 26. Wang, a Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, made her San Francisco Symphony debut in 2006 and toured Asia with the company and its former conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. She has since become a recurring guest pianist at Davies Symphony Hall and has performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, Toronto Symphony Orchestra and more. Wang is celebrated for both her stage presence and musical skills, and returns to Davies Symphony Hall next month to direct a program of 20th-century favorites by Prokofiev with the Mahler Chamber Orchestra, including Alexander Tsfasman’s Suite for Piano and Orchestra (Jazz Suite). The Mahler Chamber Orchestra is a professional touring chamber orchestra founded by Claudio Abbado and former members of the Gustav Mahler Youth Orchestra in 1997. The orchestra consists Yuja Wang of 45 musicians from 20 different nations and performs over 60 concerts a year worldwide. Matthew Truscott serves as concertmaster and leader for the evening concert. Performance begins at 7:30 p.m. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2025-26/ YUJA-WANG-MCO to purchase tickets, or call the San Francisco Symphony box office at (415) 864-6000.
articles.title: Yuja Wang & Mahler Chamber Orchestra perform at Davies Symphony Hall April 26

articles.text: The Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO), California’s oldest independent youth orchestra, presents the America 250 Festival: Celebration of American Music on Saturday, May 2, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. at First Church Berkeley. The special festival concert commemorates the 250th anniversary of the United States with an evening of chamber and orchestral works by American composers spanning more than a century of musical history. The concert also serves as YPSO’s annual Spring Concert— the third concert in its 2025–2026 subscription series. As part of nationwide celebrations of America’s 250th anniversary in 2026, the festival explores the musical traditions that have shaped the American orchestral landscape while highlighting the role of young musicians in carrying that legacy forward. Presented in an expanded festival format, the event features a first half of chamber music performed by YPSO musicians, followed by a full orchestral program. The festival highlights the diversity and creativity of American composers, from iconic figures such as Aaron Copland and Leonard Bernstein to influential contemporary voices including Jessie Montgomery, George Walker, and Kenji Bunch. The first half of the festival showcases chamber music performed by YPSO musicians in different ensembles, including strings, brass, winds, and percussion. These smaller ensembles offer audiences an intimate musical experience while allowing students to collaborate closely and explore a wide range of styles and traditions. “Chamber music encompasses important musical techniques of listening, blending, and playing together like no other musical genre,” said Julie Kim, YPSO’s Chamber Music Director. “At the America 250 Festival, we will feature several combinations of ensembles to showcase American composers at their best.” The second half of the program brings the full orchestra to the stage with a selection of works that highlight the breadth and evolution of American orchestral music across generations. “This America 250 Festival program represents a range of American voices in classical music, both chamber and symphonic, from the 20th and 21st centuries,” said Music Director David Ramadanoff. The festival program reflects more than a century of American musical creativity, featuring composers who have shaped the nation’s musical identity—from early twentieth-century pioneers to leading voices of today. This project is supported in part by a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts. Tickets are $20, while students are free (registration is required). Approximate program length: 120 minutes, including intermission. Box Office & Concert Info: www. ypsomusic.org/events. articles.title: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra celebrates America’s 250th Anniversary

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company (MTC) will celebrate six decades of theatrical work and community support with a 60th anniversary benefit gala on Sunday, April 19. The gala will honor three individuals for their contributions to the arts and to MTC Carey Perloff, recognized for her work in Bay Area theater; Vickie Soulier, a longtime supporter and former board member; and Ivan Poutiatine, a former board president and volunteer recognized for years of service. The event begins at 5 p.m. at Mill Valley Community Center and will raise funds to support the future of the theater company. Guests are invited to attend a cocktail reception followed by a seated dinner prepared by Stacy Scott Catering. The evening will also include live and silent auctions featuring travel and entertainment packages, including a weekend trip to Oregon Shakespeare Festival with theater tickets and accommodations. Entertainment during the gala will highlight Marin Theatre’s history and its work developing and presenting classic and contemporary productions. “I’m excited to bring together our community of supporters, performers and artists to commemorate this important occasion,” said Marin Theatre Executive Artistic Director Lance Gardner in a statement. “With decades of presenting top-flight professional productions of classic and modern plays and musicals and developing new works for the theatre, this remarkable artistic home has held on through thick and thin, and continues to offer enduring artistic excellence right here in Mill Valley.” The gala planning committee includes Barbara Morrison, Stacy Scott, Laura Odeh Steele, Kathleen Taylor and Penny Wright. For tickets or more information visit marintheatre.org/60thanniversary or call 415-388-5208.
articles.title: Marin Theatre Company 60th anniversary gala held April 19

articles.text: The great violinist Itzhak Perlman It was the autumn of 1891. Sherlock Holmes was at the height of his fame and immortal violinist Pablo de Sarasate was packing audiences in. In the classic story The Redheaded League Holmes invites Watson to attend a violin concert. He is interested to attend because Sarasate will play lots of German music. It is possible that the program pictured is the actual concert that Holmes and Watson attended. You see, dear readers, it was the program that was the enticement. That was frequently the case when attending concerts. Yes, there is the headliner, but the contents of the program must be interesting. What makes an interesting program? That is a very good question. When planning a program, the musician must be as adventurous as a chef preparing a fantastic meal. All too often the music is just one heavy thing after another. The same is true with dining. You should not have a heavy first and heavy main course and then follow it by a rich dessert. Indigestion can result. Musical indigestion is often caused by musical programs which feature one heavy Sonata after another. The great musicians of the past chose their programs carefully – one of the reasons they were successful. The great band leader/composer John Philip Sousa usually offered pairs of music. He would schedule two waltzes together, followed by two marches, and two polkas. He was also very open-minded and innovative with his soloists. Looking back on his programs, it was surprising at times to see the incredible variety that he offered. His imagination was limitless. Arthur Fiedler, of Boston Pops fame, was cut from the same cloth. While he was acclaimed as the conductor and director of the Boston Pops Orchestra, his fame was international. He visited San Francisco every year and presented similar programming called the San Francisco Pops. A good friend of mine was the featured soloist on one of these programs in 1964. While Fiedler was in San Francisco, he conducted the Orchestra of the Family Club. There’s even a commemorative United States postage stamp featuring Arthur Fiedler… Such was his fame. The great 19th century pianist Franz Liszt made two important changes in piano concerts. One of his changes was that he was the only soloist. Before Liszt, concerts were a type of variety show.

articles.text: Piedmont Roundup Market Observations, Insider Wisdom & The Week in Piedmont Real Estate Those of you that are attorneys may be familiar with the saying, “The wheels of justice grind slow, but grind fine” well Lady Justice hold my beer because the wheels of municipal government have the option to grind at a pace that Case in point, the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, the City of Piedmont has directed staff to move forward with a request for qualifications (RFQ) which effectively adds another six to twelve months onto the process. Think of an RFQ as a developer’s non legacy application to Stanford, Harvard, or Southern Methodist University. It is not the project itself. It is the city deciding who is allowed to apply. That is a high bar to entry, and high bars take time to clear. The next step in the process is a request for proposals (RFP). Parenthetically, my original timeline started at the RFP. The long and winding road to affordable housing in Piedmont just got longer and windier. In the News The Senate passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act by an overwhelming 89 to 10 vote, which tells you two things right away. One, housing is now a bipartisan problem. Two, Washington finally noticed that the supply side is broken. The bill is aimed at speeding up housing production, loosening some federal red tape, and limiting large institutional investors from scooping up more single-family homes while giving renters a first chance to buy. The catch is that it is not law yet. The bill still has to survive the House, where politics has a way of turning housing policy into hostage negotiation. I wrote about this for “some other outlet” but the piece is available on my blog without a pay gate. Reader Question This column’s reader question brought this quote to mind: “Advice is what we ask for when we already know the answer but wish we didn’t.” Edgar J. Schoen Question: Can I sell my house to my friend without paying my realtor her commission? Answer: You can if your listing agreement has expired or is canceled, but you need to be extremely careful about the “tail period” in your contract. Most listing agreements include a protection clause that grants the broker a commission if the property is sold to someone who was introduced to the property during the listing period—meaning if your friend popped by during an open house and used the sign-in sheet that qualifies as being introduced. Even if you cancel the agreement, that broker usually has the right to provide you with a list of names they showed the property to, and if you sell to anyone on that list within a specified timeframe (typically 30 to 90 days), you are still on the hook for that commission. If you are thinking about cutting out your realtor to save money, check your contract for that specific clause before you make a move. If your listing is still active, trying to bypass the agent is a breach of contract that can lead to a messy legal dispute. If the contract has fully expired or you have negotiated a formal, written release with the brokerage, then you are typically free to sell to whomever you want without owing a commission. A strong turnout of 49 walkers, plus two loyal K-9 companions, gathered at the Exedra, ready to combine a pleasant walk with a little market intelligence and, as always, a bit of neighborhood curiosity. After all, few things draw a Piedmonter’s interest like a “For Sale” sign. Before setting off, local real estate professionals Stacey Isaacs and Max Becker offered a snapshot of the market, equal parts perspective and reality check. Nationally, the median home price now sits just under $400,000, according to the National Association of Realtors, with Realtor.com placing it closer to $418,000. Prices have risen dramatically over the past three decades, far outpacing income growth. The result is a housing market that is significantly less accessible than it once was. Today’s buyers face larger down payments, longer saving periods, and a later entry into homeownership, with first-time buyers now averaging around age 40. Closer to home, the Piedmont market tells a more nuanced story. Home sales in 2025 were nearly identical to the previous year, 109 compared to 108, suggesting steady activity. Prices, however, continue to climb. The median home price last year was $2.68 million, and early 2026 figures suggest it is approaching $3 million. Price per square foot has also increased, and about one in four homes is selling above the asking price. Isaacs noted an interesting shift in mortgage dynamics. For the first time in years, there is now a balance between homeowners with rates above 6% and those below 3%. Buyers, it seems, are adjusting to this “new normal,” and activity remains strong. Proposition 19 is also playing a role, allowing homeowners over 55 to transfer their property tax base, making downsizing or relocating within California more attractive. She added that staging has become nearly universal in the inner East Bay, with more than 90% of homes prepared before hitting the market. The service begins at 7:30pm in the sanctuary. This is a dramatic and moving ritual. As the story of Jesus’ path to death on a cross is read out loud, candles and lights are gradually extinguished, until the entire Sanctuary is in darkness, except for one candle. At the conclusion of the service, everyone departs in silence. Easter Sunday services, celebrating the joyous resurrection of Jesus three days after his crucifixion, will be held Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am. There will be a beautiful display of Easter lilies in the Sanctuary. The services are identical and include liturgy, a sermon by Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted and special music provided by Dr. Stephen Main and the Chancel Choir. The 10am service will also be live streamed on our website at PiedmontChurch.org. You are most welcome to participate in any or all of these events. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen speaking on behalf of the City Council and Community to thank Hendry for his service I will forever be grateful for the steady hand you’ve provided over the years.” “I speak for myself, and also on behalf of the Council, and the entire community, when I say thank you, Robb, truly. For 23 years, you have shown up for us on our worst days, in times of high stress and high stakes. And every time you have shown up ready to meet the challenge, not only with professional skills and training you possess, but with your thoughtful compassion and steadfast resolve,” said Mayor Andersen. Before his career as a firefighter, Hendry attended paramedic school and worked as a paramedic. Through his studies and work, he realized he was especially good under pressure. He had a unique ability to focus and stay calm under any condition. He believed the next logical step for him was to join the fire service. Hendry joined PFD in 2003 as part of a large class of seven recruits. He is known throughout the department for his calm, focused demeanor and his commitment to exceptional patient care in every situation. “I’d like people to remember that I was honest and genuine, and I just tried to be the best version of myself that I could be,” said Hendry. Hendry intends to live the next chapter of his life like his dog. “There’s a saying: ‘Be like your dog.’ Because all your dog is doing is living in the present. My whole life has been chasing. This career is a life of jumping through hoops, uncertainty, and being on all the time. Now, I feel like I can finally be like my dog,” said Hendry. Captain Jon Fitzpatrick thanks Hendry for his service and the example he set as a model public servant. Where in the World Are We?
